section.title: The Sermon on the Mount: Beatitudes and the Law
section.sectionRationale: The first of Matthew's five great discourses opens on a mountain, where Jesus, like a new Moses, teaches the character and righteousness of the kingdom. He pronounces the surprising blessings of the Beatitudes, calls His people salt and light, declares that He came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, and then, in six contrasts, drives the commandments to their heart-deep intent.
section.thesis: Jesus unveils the life of the kingdom: a blessedness that belongs to the humble and hungry, a public witness of salt and light, and a righteousness that, far from abolishing the Law, fulfills it by reaching the heart, so that His people are called to a wholeness of love that mirrors their heavenly Father.
section.frameNote: Ten beats: Jesus sits to teach; the Beatitudes; salt and light; His coming to fulfill the Law; and six contrasts on anger, lust, divorce, oaths, retaliation, and love of enemies, ending in the call to be perfect as the Father is perfect.

units.label: On the mountain
units.note: the new Moses sits to teach

verses.text: When Jesus saw the crowds, He went up on the mountain and sat down. His disciples came to Him,
and He began to teach them, saying:

units.label: The Beatitudes
units.note: blessed are the poor in spirit

verses.text: “{{makarios|Blessed}} are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.
Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.
Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for {{dikaiosyne|righteousness}}, for they will be filled.
Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God.
Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Blessed are you when people insult you, persecute you, and falsely say all kinds of evil against you because of Me.
Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven, for in the same way they persecuted the prophets before you.
You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, how can it be made salty again? It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled by men.
You are the light of the world. A city on a hill cannot be hidden.
Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a basket. Instead, they set it on a stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house.
In the same way, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.

units.label: To fulfill the Law
units.note: not to abolish but to fulfill

verses.text: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to {{pleroo|fulfill}} them.
For I tell you truly, until heaven and earth pass away, not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen, will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished.

So then, whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do likewise will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever practices and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

units.label: Anger and reconciliation
units.note: you have heard, but I tell you

verses.text: You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘Do not murder’ and ‘Anyone who murders will be subject to judgment.’

But I tell you that anyone who is angry with his brother will be subject to judgment. Again, anyone who says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be subject to the Sanhedrin. But anyone who says, ‘You fool!’ will be subject to the fire of hell.
So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you,
leave your gift there before the altar. First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.

Reconcile quickly with your adversary, while you are still on the way to court. Otherwise, he may hand you over to the judge, and the judge may hand you over to the officer, and you may be thrown into prison.
Truly I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the last penny.
You have heard that it was said, ‘Do not commit adultery.’
But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
If your right eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into hell.
And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to depart into hell.
It has also been said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce.’
But I tell you that anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, brings adultery upon her. And he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
Again, you have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘Do not break your oath, but fulfill your vows to the Lord.’
But I tell you not to swear at all: either by heaven, for it is God’s throne;
or by the earth, for it is His footstool; or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.
Nor should you swear by your head, for you cannot make a single hair white or black.
Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’ Anything more comes from the evil one.
You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye and tooth for tooth.’
But I tell you not to resist an evil person. If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also;
if someone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well;
and if someone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles.
Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.

units.label: Love your enemies
units.note: be perfect as your Father is perfect

verses.text: You have heard that it was said, ‘Love your neighbor’ and ‘Hate your enemy.’
But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,
that you may be sons of your Father in heaven. He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.
If you love those who love you, what reward will you get? Do not even tax collectors do the same?
And if you greet only your brothers, what are you doing more than others? Do not even Gentiles do the same?
Be {{teleios|perfect}}, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.

makarios.gloss: Blessed, happy, flourishing in God's favor. Not a wish but a declaration: Jesus pronounces the truly fortunate to be the poor in spirit, the mourning, the meek, a stunning reversal of the world's idea of the good life.

dikaiosyne.gloss: Righteousness, right conduct and right standing before God. In the Sermon it is both hungered for as a gift and lived out as obedience; the kingdom righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees by reaching the heart.

pleroo.gloss: To fill up, complete, fulfill. Jesus did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them, bringing them to their intended goal in Himself and in the deeper obedience of the heart He teaches.

teleios.gloss: Complete, whole, mature, perfect. The call to be perfect as the Father is perfect is a call to undivided, all-embracing love that reflects God's own character, the summit toward which the whole chapter climbs.

basic.context: Jesus climbs a mountain, sits down like a teacher, and delivers the most famous sermon ever preached. He begins with the Beatitudes, declaring the truly blessed to be the humble, mourning, and hungry, the opposite of what the world admires. He calls His followers salt and light, insists He came to fulfill the law rather than cancel it, and then, in six pointed contrasts, shows that God's commands reach the heart, not just outward behavior.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the Beatitudes as descriptions of the character God's grace produces in kingdom people, not as a ladder to climb. Read the six statements that begin You have heard, but I tell you not as Jesus correcting Moses but as Him exposing the true, heart-deep intent of the law against shallow readings. The whole sermon shows the righteousness of the kingdom, which only Christ can give and empower.
basic.originalLanguages: Blessed means truly flourishing in God's favor, and Jesus declares it over surprising people. The key word righteousness runs through the sermon: it is both hungered for and lived out, and it must exceed that of the religious experts. Jesus comes to fulfill the law, to bring it to its goal, and He calls His people to be perfect, whole and complete in love, as their Father is.
basic.typology: Jesus is the new and greater Moses, giving the law of the kingdom from a mountain as Moses gave the law from Sinai, yet with an authority Moses never claimed: I tell you. His people are the light of the world, the role Israel was meant to play among the nations, now taken up in Christ.
basic.christ: Jesus speaks with a startling personal authority, setting His word above what was said to the ancients and making loyalty to Himself the measure of blessing. He is the one who truly fulfills the law, the only one who perfectly embodies the righteousness He describes. He alone lives the Beatitudes fully, and by His Spirit He forms them in His people.
basic.god: The sermon reveals a Father who blesses the humble, rewards the persecuted, and pours sun and rain on the evil and the good alike. His character is the standard: His people are to be merciful, pure, peacemaking, and loving toward enemies because that is what He is like. His kingdom turns the world's values upside down.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 37 lies behind the meek inheriting the earth. Isaiah 61 shapes the blessing on those who mourn. Leviticus 19 gives love your neighbor, which Jesus extends to enemies. And Romans 13 says love fulfills the law, echoing the sermon's heart.
basic.oneStory: On the mountain the King describes life under His reign. The blessings He pronounces overturn every worldly measure of success, and the righteousness He requires goes deeper than any rule-keeping, all the way to the heart. No one can live this but Christ, who fulfills the law for us and, by His Spirit, begins to shape His own character in His people until they love as their Father loves.

context.literary:
Matthew 5 is the first of three chapters that make up the Sermon on the Mount, and it is a tightly built piece of teaching. A narrative frame opens it, 'He went up on the mountain and sat down,' verse 1, and a matching frame closes the whole sermon, 'the crowds were astonished at His teaching, because He taught as one who had authority,' Matthew 7:28-29. Inside, the chapter moves through four blocks: the Beatitudes, verses 3 to 12; the two images of salt and light, verses 13 to 16; the statement on the Law and the Prophets, verses 17 to 20; and six contrasts, verses 21 to 48.

The Beatitudes are carefully made. The first and eighth end with the same promise, 'theirs is the kingdom of heaven,' verses 3 and 10, and this framing, together with the present tense of both, shows that the kingdom already belongs to these people. The ones in between are future: comforted, inherit, filled, shown mercy, see God, called sons of God. In the Greek the first four describing words begin with the same letter, which gives the opening a drumbeat that English cannot copy. Verses 11 and 12 turn from 'those who' to 'you,' addressing the disciples directly.

The six contrasts share a fixed formula, 'You have heard that it was said' followed by 'But I tell you.' The first three deal with anger, lust and divorce, and the next three with oaths, retaliation and love of enemies. Each moves from an outward act to an inward source. The verses on the Law in verses 17 to 20 act as the hinge, announcing the thesis, a righteousness that 'exceeds' that of the scribes and Pharisees, and the contrasts then show what the exceeding looks like. The final verse, 'Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect,' closes the whole chapter with the standard behind all six.
context.historical:
Matthew places the sermon on 'the mountain,' a hillside in Galilee that he does not name. Teachers in that world sat to teach, and standing was for reading Scripture. Sitting down signals that what follows is formal, authoritative instruction. Many readers also see Moses behind the scene, who went up Mount Sinai to receive the Law, and the setting makes Jesus' teaching a new giving of the will of God. Matthew is careful to say that the disciples came to Him, but the crowds were within earshot, as Matthew 7:28 shows.

The first hearers lived under foreign rule and in a religious world that took the Law very seriously. The scribes were the experts in the Law, and the Pharisees were a movement that sought to apply it carefully to ordinary life. Jesus' remark in verse 20 about a righteousness that exceeds theirs would have been startling, since they were regarded as the most devout people around.

Several customs lie behind the examples. A hand struck on the right cheek was most likely a backhand blow, which was more an insult than an injury. A creditor could take a man's tunic through a court, but the cloak was protected in the Law, Exodus 22:26-27, so Jesus' picture of giving up even the cloak goes past what the Law could demand. Roman soldiers could compel civilians to carry their loads for a mile, and the verb Matthew uses is the one used when Simon of Cyrene was forced to carry the cross, Matthew 27:32.

The word that the BSB translates 'hell' in verses 22, 29 and 30 is Gehenna, named for the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where the people of Judah once burned their children, Jeremiah 7:31-32. By Jesus' day it had become a picture of final judgment. A certificate of divorce, verse 31, refers to Deuteronomy 24:1, and in the Jewish debate of the time the question was how wide the grounds should be.
context.canonical:
The Sermon on the Mount draws on the whole Old Testament. The Beatitudes read like the poems of the Psalms and the prophets. Psalm 37:11 stands behind the meek who inherit, Isaiah 61:1-3 behind the comfort of those who mourn, Psalm 24:3-4 behind the pure in heart who see God, and Isaiah 57:15 and 66:2 behind God's regard for the lowly and contrite. The first Psalm begins with a blessing, 'Blessed is the man,' Psalm 1:1, and the Beatitudes carry on that wisdom tradition with a surprising answer to the question of who is blessed.

Salt and light connect to Israel's calling. Isaiah told Zion, 'Arise, shine, for your light has come,' and promised that 'Nations will come to your light,' Isaiah 60:1-3, and the Servant is called 'a light to the nations,' Isaiah 42:6. Jesus gives the role to His disciples. The city on a hill recalls the same prophetic picture of Zion.

The six contrasts quote the Ten Commandments (murder, adultery), the Law of divorce, Leviticus 19:12 on oaths, the rule of retaliation in Exodus 21:24 and Leviticus 24:20, and Leviticus 19:18 on loving the neighbour. The closing call to perfection echoes 'You must be blameless before the LORD your God,' Deuteronomy 18:13, and 'Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy,' Leviticus 19:2. Luke's version, 'Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful,' Luke 6:36, gives the same idea in different words.

Later Scripture develops the sermon's themes. Paul says love is the fulfilment of the law, Romans 13:8-10 and Galatians 5:14, and tells believers, 'Bless those who persecute you,' Romans 12:14. James repeats Jesus' teaching on oaths, James 5:12. Peter sets out how Christ did not retaliate when abused, 1 Peter 2:23. The promise of the new covenant that makes such living possible is found in Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26-27, and Paul says that in those who walk by the Spirit 'the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled,' Romans 8:4.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew gives this sermon to show what life under the reign of Jesus looks like and to answer a question that hung over his readers: how does the kingdom relate to the Law? Some would have supposed that a Messiah who brought the kingdom would sweep the old commands away; others, that the scribes and Pharisees, with their careful rules, already held the true standard. Jesus' answer is that the Law stands, and that He brings it to its full meaning, so that the standard rises, not falls.

The Beatitudes are meant to turn the readers' picture of blessing upside down. The people Jesus calls blessed are those the world overlooks, and the blessing is anchored in the coming of the kingdom, not in present comfort. The disciples are to know that persecution, when it comes because of Jesus, puts them in the company of the prophets, verse 12.

The six contrasts have a single aim. Jesus is not setting His own rules against Moses'; He is exposing what the commandments were always about. Murder starts in anger, adultery in the look, false oaths in a heart that cannot be trusted to speak plainly, and revenge in a refusal to trust God to judge. The goal is a people whose goodness goes all the way through, so that they look like their Father. In this way Matthew calls his readers to a righteousness greater than the religion of mere appearances.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The sermon is both description and command, and it is important to read each part in its form. The Beatitudes are declarations about who is blessed; they describe what God's grace produces and promises, and they do not give a checklist for earning the kingdom. The commands in the contrasts, however, are real commands, and the verbs are imperatives: be reconciled, do not swear, turn the other cheek, love your enemies.

The vivid examples need careful handling. The instruction to gouge out an eye or cut off a hand in verses 29 and 30 uses deliberate exaggeration to teach that sin must be dealt with at any cost; the church has never taken it to require self-mutilation, and Jesus Himself makes clear in Matthew 15:19 that evil comes out of the heart, which no amputation can reach. Likewise, the commands about the cheek, the cloak and the second mile illustrate a spirit of non-retaliation and generosity; they are not a rule that abolishes courts, police or the care of the vulnerable, since Romans 13 recognises a governing authority and Jesus does not here address the duties of a magistrate.

What we are to take from these verses is a way of life: a heart-level righteousness, a readiness to absorb wrongs rather than avenge them, and a love that does not stop at the border of those who love us. That is for every disciple, and we are to seek it by the Spirit and not by effort alone.

debates.question: What does Jesus mean by fulfilling the Law and the Prophets?

views.label: Bringing the law to its intended goal in Himself
views.case: Jesus completes what the law and prophets pointed toward, embodying and accomplishing their aim; He does not discard the Old Testament but brings it to fruition in His person and teaching.

views.label: Establishing the law's true, heart-deep meaning
views.case: Fulfilling includes teaching and living out the full, God-intended sense of the commandments against shallow readings, so that the deeper righteousness of the heart is upheld, not lowered.

debates.bearing: Both guard against two errors, that Jesus abolishes the Old Testament or that He merely repeats it; He brings it to its goal and reveals its depth, and only in Him is it truly kept.

debates.question: How are the demands to turn the cheek, love enemies, and be perfect to be lived?

views.label: A real ethic of the kingdom, empowered by grace
views.case: Jesus genuinely calls His people to non-retaliation and enemy-love as the Spirit-shaped life of the kingdom, reflecting the Father who blesses the evil and the good; it is demanding but meant to be lived.

views.label: An ideal that also exposes sin and drives us to Christ
views.case: The height of the standard, culminating in be perfect, shows no one can attain it by self-effort, humbling us, revealing our need of grace, and sending us to the Savior who alone fulfilled it.

debates.bearing: Both are true together: the Sermon is a real way of life for the redeemed and a mirror that drives self-righteous hearts to depend wholly on Christ.

debates.question: Does the 'exception clause' in verse 32 allow divorce and remarriage?

views.label: Divorce is permitted for sexual immorality, and the innocent party may remarry
views.case: Jesus names one ground, porneia, and Matthew 19:9 repeats it. Since a divorce for that cause really ends the marriage, many hold that the innocent partner is free to remarry. This has been the main Protestant reading since the Reformation.

views.label: The exception allows separation but not remarriage
views.case: Some, including many in the older church, take the exception to permit only a legal separation, because Jesus appeals to the creation order that 'the two will become one flesh,' Matthew 19:5-6, which God has joined and man must not divide.

views.label: The exception names a different offence
views.case: A few read porneia as a reference to an unlawful union within the forbidden degrees of kinship, so that Jesus is speaking of a marriage that was never valid. The wording of the passage is used to defend this, though most scholars are not convinced.

debates.bearing: All three agree that Jesus rejects easy divorce and sets marriage in the context of God's purpose from creation. The church should treat marriage with the seriousness Jesus shows, and handle painful cases with both truth and compassion.

debates.question: In what sense does the Law remain in force, verses 18 and 19?

views.label: Its authority stays, fulfilled in Christ
views.case: Jesus says that not a stroke will disappear 'until everything is accomplished,' and later teaches that all the Law and Prophets point to Him, Luke 24:44. The Law remains true and authoritative but is now read through Christ, who brings it to its goal, Romans 10:4.

views.label: The moral law continues unchanged, while the ceremonial law is fulfilled
views.case: Reformed teachers have distinguished moral, civil and ceremonial parts. The moral commands still bind believers, while sacrifices and the temple are fulfilled in Christ. The six contrasts, they say, deal with moral commands.

views.label: The Law is fulfilled by the new teaching of Jesus
views.case: Some stress that Jesus' own word becomes the standard, so that the Law is kept by following His teaching. This sees the sermon as the authoritative interpretation of the Law for the new age.

debates.bearing: Each view insists that Jesus does not discard the Law and that obedience matters. They differ on how to apply individual commands, but all see Christ as the one who fulfils the Law and whose Spirit enables its heart to be lived.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of the Beatitudes names the poor. The word is ptochos, which in the Greek of the day means the destitute, the beggar who has nothing and depends on others. It differs from the word for a person who works for little. Matthew adds 'in spirit' and so makes it plain that the poverty is before God: it is the recognition of one's own bankruptcy. Luke has a simpler 'poor,' Luke 6:20, and the two accounts complement each other.

The word for 'meek,' praus, describes a gentle strength, not weakness. Jesus uses it of Himself when He says, 'I am gentle and humble in heart,' Matthew 11:29, and the promise 'they will inherit the earth' follows the wording of Psalm 37:11. The word translated 'earth' can also mean 'land,' so the hearer of the Psalm would hear the old promise of the inheritance, now widened.

The call to be salt and light uses a striking verb. If salt 'loses its savor,' the Greek says it becomes foolish, moranthe, the root of our word moron. In the original the flavour is not lost; the salt has gone senseless. The 'basket' under which no one hides a lamp is a modios, a grain measure, so the picture is of an ordinary household vessel.

In verse 17 the verb 'abolish' is katalyo, which means to loosen down, to demolish a building. Jesus says He has not come to take the Law apart. The 'jot' is the smallest letter of the alphabet, and the 'stroke' is literally a little horn, the tiny projection that marks one letter from another. This is a way of saying that even the smallest detail of Scripture matters.

Verse 22 contains the Aramaic insult 'Raca,' probably a term of contempt for an empty-headed person, followed by 'You fool,' moros. The punishments rise with the insults: judgment, the Sanhedrin, and the Gehenna of fire. Jesus is not setting a table of penalties; He is showing that contempt for a person is the same kind of thing as murder, only in a smaller form.

Verse 32 uses porneia for the exception. It is a broad word for sexual immorality and not the more specific word for adultery, which accounts for the difference in debates about its meaning. In verse 39 the verb for 'resist' is antistenai, to stand against, and the phrase 'an evil person' could also be read 'the evil one.' Jesus' point is that His followers do not meet harm with a matching harm. The word for 'forces' in verse 41, angareuo, was borrowed into Greek from Persian, where it described the royal courier's right to press others into service.

The command in verse 44 is agapao, the love that gives itself for another's good, and the word is the same as in verse 43, where Jesus quotes the neighbour command. The text 'hate your enemy' does not appear in the Law, though the Law does say to help an enemy's fallen animal, Exodus 23:4-5. Jesus is correcting a common inference, not Moses.

typology.type: The mountain and the new Moses
typology.fulfillment: Moses went up Sinai to receive the Law and came down to the people; Jesus goes up a mountain, sits as a teacher, and speaks with His own authority. His formula 'But I tell you' stands against 'it was said,' something no prophet had done, for prophets said 'Thus says the LORD.' The crowds saw the difference, 'He taught as one who had authority,' Matthew 7:29. The escalation is that Moses gave the Law from God, while Jesus speaks as the One whose Law it is. The correspondence has a limit: Jesus does not stand between two parties as a mediator who might fail; He is the Son who makes the new covenant, Jeremiah 31:33.

typology.type: Israel's calling as light to the nations
typology.fulfillment: Israel was set apart to be a light to the nations, Isaiah 42:6 and 60:3, and the city on a hill suggests Zion, to which the nations would stream. In Matthew 5:14 Jesus says that His disciples are the light of the world, and in John 8:12 He claims the same title for Himself, so that the disciples' light is borrowed from Him. The type is fulfilled in a community formed around Christ and sent to all nations, Matthew 28:19. It falls short where Israel's light was tied to a particular place and nation; the disciples carry theirs wherever they go.

The Law was always meant to shape the heart, as when it says 'You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart,' Leviticus 19:17. The contrasts in verses 21 to 48 draw out that inward intent, and the prophets promised a day when God would 'inscribe it on their hearts,' Jeremiah 31:33, and give a new heart and His Spirit, Ezekiel 36:26-27. In Jesus' teaching the promised inwardness is exposed, and in His work it is made possible, since His Spirit is given to His people, Romans 8:4. The type is not complete in this chapter, for the sermon shows the standard and the cross and Spirit provide the power.

Jesus says His followers will be persecuted 'in the same way' as the prophets before them, verse 12, and the Old Testament is full of prophets who suffered for speaking God's word, Jeremiah and Elijah among them. The pattern is carried to its peak in Jesus Himself, who is the final Prophet and the one persecuted without cause. The reward is the same: great reward in heaven. The type reaches its fulfilment because suffering for Christ brings the disciple into the story of the Servant, who 'did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23.

study.christ:
The sermon leads to Christ first by its authority. The phrase 'But I tell you' is the voice of someone who stands above Moses, not against him. He does not cite rabbis or prophets; He speaks as the one whose word is the final test. By setting loyalty to Himself as the measure of blessing, 'because of Me,' verse 11, He claims a place that only God can claim. Matthew records the crowd's astonishment, because He taught 'as one who had authority,' Matthew 7:29.

It leads to Christ by fulfilment. When He says He has come 'to fulfill' the Law and the Prophets, He claims that all of Scripture's promises and patterns find their meaning in Him. He later says that everything written about Him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled, Luke 24:44. He is the only person who has kept every commandment from the heart. He is the poor in spirit who depended on the Father, the one who mourned over Jerusalem, the meek one who rode into the city on a donkey, the merciful one, the pure in heart, the peacemaker who made peace by His blood, and the persecuted one who prayed for the men who crucified Him. In each beatitude the reader may see His face.

It leads to Christ by contrast with our failure. A reader who takes the sermon seriously finds that no one has loved enemies perfectly, never looked with desire, never spoken a careless word. The standard that closes the chapter, 'Be perfect,' brings the same conclusion that Paul reaches, that the Law was 'our guardian to lead us to Christ,' Galatians 3:24. The sermon does not stop there, because the same Christ offers the way out. 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21.

It leads to Christ by what He supplies. The righteousness the kingdom needs is not just the standard He sets but the gift He gives. The hunger and thirst for righteousness in verse 6 will be filled, and Isaiah's invitation, 'Come, all you who are thirsty,' Isaiah 55:1, is answered by the One who says, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary,' Matthew 11:28. In the new covenant He pours out the Spirit so that 'the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us,' Romans 8:4. Jesus' own conduct under insult, 'He did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23, shows what the sermon looks like when it is lived.

A caution keeps this honest. The sermon is not only a mirror to drive us to Christ, and it is not only a code to follow; it is both a description of kingdom life and a call to seek it from the King. We should not allegorise the details, treating the mountain or the salt as hidden pictures of Jesus; the christological weight lies in who is speaking and what He claims, and in what He accomplishes for people who cannot meet the standard on their own.
study.god:
The sermon's picture of God is that of a Father, the word that Jesus uses with growing frequency through these chapters. The Father is 'in heaven,' reigning, and yet near enough that His children are to show His character. He is the one whose reward awaits the persecuted, verse 12, who is glorified by the good deeds of His people, verse 16, and whose own perfection is the pattern for theirs, verse 48.

It shows a God of holy and exacting character. His commands are not arbitrary rules but the expression of who He is. The Law's depth, reaching to anger, desire, speech and revenge, shows that He judges the heart. The warnings of Gehenna in the contrasts are as real as the promises of the Beatitudes, and the passage does not allow us to soften either. The God who blesses the poor in spirit is the God who will not tolerate contempt for a brother.

It shows a God who is generous beyond what is deserved. 'He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous,' verse 45. This is the doctrine of common grace in a single sentence: the ordinary mercies of daily life are given to people whether or not they honour Him, and His love for enemies is the model for ours. Luke puts it in terms of mercy, 'Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful,' Luke 6:36.

It shows a God who is faithful to His word. Not a stroke of the Law will vanish until everything is accomplished, verse 18. God does not revise His standards when it becomes inconvenient, and He does not forget what He promised. The Law and the Prophets are fulfilled, not discarded, because the same God spoke them.

It shows a God who is a judge and a reconciler together. The picture of leaving a gift at the altar to be reconciled with a brother, verses 23 and 24, makes worship dependent on peace with others, so that God cares about how we treat people as much as how we approach Him. His justice and mercy do not conflict.

For worship, the sermon shows us how to come: with empty hands, aware of our poverty, hungry for a righteousness we do not have, and glad to be called His children. It asks that our praise not be separated from our relationships, and it invites us to trust a Father whose character is the final standard of goodness and whose love is wide enough to include the enemy. The God of the Beatitudes gives the kingdom to the poor in spirit, and He gives it freely.

crossReferences.note: The source of the third beatitude. The psalm contrasts the wicked who seem to prosper with the meek who 'will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity.' Jesus applies the promise to all who are gentle before God, and 'land' widens to the whole earth, the inheritance of a people under His reign.

The prophet speaks of one anointed 'to comfort all who mourn' and to give 'a crown of beauty for ashes.' The second beatitude's comfort for mourners draws on this passage, and Jesus later reads Isaiah 61 as being about Himself, Luke 4:18-21, so the comfort promised in the sermon is given by the one the prophet announced.

Asks who may stand in the LORD's holy place and answers, 'He who has clean hands and a pure heart.' The sixth beatitude, 'the pure in heart will see God,' takes up this entrance question and pushes it inward: the requirement is not ritual cleanness but a heart without division.

God says, 'This is the one I will esteem: he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word.' This stands behind the first beatitude's 'poor in spirit.' The kingdom is given to those who come to God with nothing of their own and take Him at His word.

The text that stands behind verse 43. It forbids hatred in the heart and revenge, and commands 'love your neighbor as yourself.' Jesus quotes the command and rejects the phrase 'hate your enemy' that had been added to it. The Law's own heart-level concern is what He draws out.

Contains 'eye for eye, tooth for tooth,' the rule Jesus cites in verse 38. In context it limits punishment to what fits the injury, a restraint on vengeance in the courts. Jesus carries the restraint further, telling His followers not to use the principle as a personal licence for payback.

The passage on the certificate of divorce, quoted in verse 31. It assumes that divorce happens and regulates it. Jesus takes up the debate about what counts as 'indecency,' and appeals to the creation order in Matthew 19:3-9, where He says Moses permitted divorce because of hard hearts.

Paul says that 'love is the fulfillment of the law,' and that the commandments about adultery, murder, theft and coveting are summed up in love of neighbour. It is the apostolic reading of what Jesus did in the six contrasts, bringing each commandment back to the love that lies behind it.

Luke's parallel sermon gives the Beatitudes, woes, love of enemies and the call to be merciful as the Father is merciful. Comparing the two helps explain Matthew's 'perfect': the content is a likeness to the Father's compassion, and not a counsel of flawless performance.

James repeats Jesus' teaching on oaths almost word for word: 'let your Yes be yes, and your No, no.' It shows that the early church received the sermon as binding instruction and applied it, and that plain honesty was seen as a mark of those under the kingdom.

Paul says that God has done what the law could not, sending His Son so that 'the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us.' This is the answer to the question the sermon raises. The standard is met in believers by the Spirit through Christ, not by their own strength.

The promise of the new covenant: 'I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts.' The sermon's call to a righteousness of the heart is the shape of that promise, and its fulfilment is the work Christ and His Spirit begin in His people.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with people made to reflect God's character on the earth, Genesis 1:26-27, and goes wrong when they refuse. Israel is then chosen to be God's treasured nation, given the Law at Sinai, and told to be holy as He is holy, Leviticus 19:2. The calling is to be a light to the nations, but the history is of failure to keep the covenant. Prophets point forward to a new covenant, where the Law is on the heart and the Spirit is poured out.

The Sermon on the Mount is the moment when the King of that covenant describes His people. It looks back and answers the question of what the Law was for. It was never a ladder to climb, and it was never just a set of outward rules; it was meant to form a people like their God. The Beatitudes announce who will receive the kingdom: not the proud and self-sufficient but the poor, the grieving, the hungry. The six contrasts show the shape of a restored humanity, in which anger, lust, deceit, revenge and hatred have no place.

It also sets up much of what follows. The righteousness that exceeds the Pharisees' requires something no one can produce on their own, and Matthew's story heads to the cross, where Jesus bears the failure of those who cannot meet it, and to the gift of the Spirit, who writes the law on the heart. The call to love enemies is seen when Jesus prays for those who crucify Him. In the early church, believers who bless their persecutors, as in Romans 12:14, show that the sermon can be lived.

The goal is a people who are the light of the world, and the end is the new creation. John says 'we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is,' 1 John 3:2, and that promise answers the sixth beatitude: the pure in heart will see God. Revelation closes the picture: 'They will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. The poor in spirit have the kingdom, the mourners are comforted, the meek inherit the earth, and the peacemakers are called the sons of God. The hunger of verse 6 is satisfied at last, and a family that looks like its Father fills a renewed world.

quiz.q: Who does Jesus say are blessed in the Beatitudes?

options.text: The poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, and those who hunger for righteousness.
options.note: Verses 3-10 pronounce blessing on the humble and hungry, reversing worldly values.

options.text: Those who are persecuted for righteousness, above all others.
options.note: The persecuted are blessed, but this is one of several Beatitudes, not the whole picture.

options.text: The wealthy, the powerful, and the successful.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus blesses the humble and needy, not the powerful and rich.

options.text: Only those who keep the whole law perfectly.
options.note: The Beatitudes bless the poor in spirit and hungry, not the self-sufficient law-keeper.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say about His relationship to the Law and the Prophets?

options.text: He came not to abolish them but to fulfill them.
options.note: Verse 17 states plainly that Jesus fulfills the law rather than cancels it.

options.text: He came to establish the law's deeper, heart-level meaning.
options.note: True as part of what fulfillment means, but the direct statement is that He fulfills, not abolishes.

options.text: He came to replace the old law with entirely new rules.
options.note: He fulfills and deepens the law; He does not simply replace it with new rules.

options.text: He came to set the law aside as no longer relevant.
options.note: He explicitly denies abolishing the law; not a jot will pass away.

quiz.q: How does Jesus deepen the command against murder?

options.text: He traces murder back to anger and contempt in the heart, which are also under judgment.
options.note: Verses 21-22 show the command reaches the heart's anger, not just the outward act.

options.text: He teaches that only physical killing is truly sinful.
options.note: The opposite; He extends the command inward to anger, not just the physical act.

options.text: He abolishes the command against murder altogether.
options.note: He does not abolish it; He deepens it to include anger and contempt.

options.text: He says murder is acceptable if the person deserves it.
options.note: He intensifies the command; nothing here excuses murder or contempt.

quiz.q: What does Jesus command regarding enemies?

options.text: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, reflecting the Father.
options.note: Verses 44-45 command enemy-love as the mark of the Father's children.

options.text: Do not take personal revenge, but you may still despise them.
options.note: He goes further than refraining from revenge; He commands active love and prayer, not mere restraint.

options.text: Love only those who love you in return.
options.note: Jesus rejects this as no better than the tax collectors; He commands love of enemies.

options.text: Hate your enemies as the tradition allowed.
options.note: Jesus directly overturns hate your enemy, commanding love instead.

quiz.q: What is the point of the closing call to be perfect as the Father is perfect?

options.text: A call to whole, undivided love that reflects God's own character.
options.note: Verse 48 caps the section on love, calling for a completeness of love like the Father's.

options.text: A demand for flawless behavior achievable by hard effort.
options.note: It calls for God-like wholeness of love, but as grace-shaped character, not self-made flawlessness; this misses the source.

options.text: A suggestion that only a few elite disciples can attain.
options.note: It is addressed to all disciples as the Father's children, not an elite few.

options.text: A statement that God does not really expect any change in us.
options.note: The call clearly summons real, Godward transformation, not indifference to change.

questions: The Beatitudes call the poor in spirit and those who mourn blessed. How does Jesus' picture of the good life challenge the way you measure success and blessing?

Jesus said the righteousness of the kingdom reaches the heart, not just outward behavior. Where is God exposing an attitude, anger, lust, or contempt, that looks fine on the surface but needs to change within?
You are the salt of the earth and the light of the world. In what setting is God calling you to let your light shine so that others glorify your Father?
Jesus commands love and prayer even for enemies. Who is the hardest person for you to love right now, and what would it look like to pray for them this week?
The whole sermon is first a portrait of Christ, who alone lived it. How does seeing your inability to keep it drive you to depend on Him for both forgiveness and power to change?

translationNotes.note: The meek may also be rendered those who exercise strength under control, and inherit the earth as inherit the land, echoing Psalm 37:11.
Raca is an Aramaic term of contempt; the fire of hell renders Gehenna, the valley outside Jerusalem that became an image of final judgment. Some manuscripts add without cause after angry.
Except for sexual immorality preserves a recognized ground; brings adultery upon her may also be rendered causes her to commit adultery, as the BSB footnote notes.
